steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The research found that a dessert on a white plate tasted about ten per cent sweeter than the same dessert on a black one.
steps.prompt: What does that finding imply about the word 'taste'?
options: That people cannot be trusted to report what they taste.
That what we call taste is assembled from several senses at once, so changing what is seen changes what is tasted.
That white plates should be used in all restaurants.
steps.answer: That what we call taste is assembled from several senses at once, so changing what is seen changes what is tasted.
steps.why: Nothing about the dessert changed. If the reported taste still changed, the sense of taste alone was never producing it.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: The recording says noisy packets 'don't make the crisps last any longer, but they do add to the sensation of crunchiness'.
steps.prompt: Why the emphatic do?
options: Because the speaker is unsure whether the effect is real.
Because a claim has just been denied, and the emphatic form marks the part that survives the denial.
Because it is more formal than they add.
steps.answer: Because a claim has just been denied, and the emphatic form marks the part that survives the denial.
steps.why: Emphatic do almost always answers something: an expectation, a doubt, or as here, the negative clause immediately before it.

steps.title: What you receive, and what you direct
steps.html:
Recycled, and set out properly, because these are wrong in almost every B2 essay.

See and hear are about receiving. They happen whether you meant them to or not, and they are not usually used in the continuous: I see a mistake. I can hear something. Never I am seeing a mistake in this meaning.

Look at and listen to are about directing. You choose to do them, and both need their preposition when an object follows: Look at this. Listen to me. Without an object, no preposition: Look! Listen!

Watch is directed and continuous: you follow something that moves or changes over time. Watch the animals. Watch television. You see a film once; you watch it while it happens.

The five looking verbs differ by manner and length: glance at (very quick), look at (neutral), stare at (long, fixed), gaze at (long, absorbed), glare at (angry).

Common collocations to learn whole: see the point, see what you mean, look forward to, look after, watch out, watch your step, hear from somebody, hear about something, listen out for.

One exception worth knowing: see IS used in the continuous when it means meet — I'm seeing the doctor at four — which is a different verb, really.

steps.title: Choosing between the five looking verbs
steps.html:
1. The situation: somebody looks at a coat in the street.
  2. If it is a fraction of a second: She glanced at the coat.
  3. If it is neutral and deliberate: She looked at the coat.
  4. If it is long and fixed, and slightly rude: She stared at the coat. This is what everybody in the recording does.
  5. If it is long and absorbed, with no rudeness: She gazed at the coat. And if she is angry: She glared at the person wearing it. All five take at.

steps.title: Write your piece.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least four of: see, look at, watch, glance at, stare at, gaze at, glare at, hear, listen to — each correctly.
steps.html:
• Open with the sense that arrives first.
  • Use at least two of the looking verbs, correctly.
  • Use <i>hear</i> or <i>listen to</i> in the right one of the two meanings.
  • Close with what surprises you about the memory.

Useful language

  • I can still hear / smell / taste …
  • If you listen to … while you eat … ,
  • Everybody stared at / glanced at …
  • It enables you to distinguish between … and …
  • Most of what we call taste is actually aroma.
  • I didn't see the point of it until …
steps.modelHtml:
My grandmother's kitchen, in winter

I cannot walk past a bakery in December without being back in it. The smell arrives first and everything else follows: the clatter of the oven door, the particular sourness of the bread she made, the fact that you were not allowed to open the fridge after four o'clock.

She used to glare at anybody who ate standing up, and she stared at me for a full ten seconds the first time I put ketchup on anything. I still cannot do it.

What surprises me now is how little of that memory is taste. It is aroma, and sound, and the sight of a particular yellow bowl. If I listen to a certain radio programme I can almost smell the kitchen, which makes no sense at all and happens every time.
